Farther means faster, and the points fall close to a straight line. Every distant galaxy is moving away from us, and a galaxy twice as far leaves about twice as fast. That is what an expanding universe looks like from inside it. Think of dots drawn on a rubber band, one centimetre apart, and stretch the band to one and a half times its length in one second. Seen from your dot, the dot that was 1 cm away is now at 1.5 cm: it moved 0.5 cm. The dot that was 4 cm away is now at 6 cm: it moved 2 cm, in the same second, so four times as far means four times as fast. Stand on any other dot and you see the same thing. No dot is the centre; the band is simply stretching everywhere.

How fast the universe is expanding is the slope of that line: how many km/s of speed each megaparsec of distance adds. So the measurement you need is the slope of the best straight line through these dots, and section 2 teaches how to find it.

Judging by eye is not enough. Two guesses that both look close cannot be told apart by looking. To choose between them you need a number that says how badly a line misses its points.

A residual is the real value minus the line's value.

$$\text{residual} = \text{real value} - \text{the line's value}$$

Take the first supernova in the table, SN1990O, 134.7 Mpc away at 9,065 km/s, and a reasonable guess, $a = 72$ and $b = 300$. The line gives it $72 \times 134.7 + 300 = 9,998$ km/s. Its residual for that line is $9,065 - 9,998 = -933$ km/s: the point sits that far below the line. A point above the line has a positive residual.

To judge a whole line with one number, use the root mean squared error, RMSE. A line has thirty-six residuals. Square each one, so that misses above and below the line cannot cancel; take the mean of the squares; take the square root, which brings the number back to km/s:

$$\text{RMSE} = \sqrt{\text{mean of the squared residuals}}$$

The RMSE is the typical miss of the line, in the units of the data. Try it on three residuals, 2, −2 and 1. Added as they are they give 1, as if the line hardly missed. Their squares are 4, 4 and 1, the mean is 3, and the square root of 3 is 1.7. In Python the square root is a power of one half: (mean) ** 0.5. Squaring makes a line care most about its worst misses; the number a fit tries to make small is also called its loss. The next cell scores your four guesses, and the example line.

    guess_rmse = ((guess_residuals ** 2).mean()) ** 0.5                     # square, average, square root
    print("a =", a, " b =", b, "  RMSE =", round(guess_rmse), "km/s")

The picture is a valley. Every pair in the dark band is a good line, and the band runs diagonally: a steeper line can be made nearly as good by starting it lower. The lowest point is $a = 67$, $b = 800$, with an RMSE of 943 km/s. Finding it this way is called least squares: the line with the smallest RMSE is the line with the smallest total of squared residuals, the same thing.

Trying every pair works, but it is slow and it only finds pairs on the grid. For a straight line there is a formula that goes to the bottom of the valley directly.

The formula. Call the distances $x_1, \ldots, x_n$ and the speeds $y_1, \ldots, y_n$, with $n = 36$, and let $\bar{x}$ and $\bar{y}$ be their averages. The $a$ and $b$ with the smallest RMSE are

$$a = \frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}, \qquad b = \bar{y} - a\,\bar{x}$$

The top of $a$ adds up, over the points, how far each one is from the average in $x$ times how far it is in $y$: positive when the two go together. The bottom is how spread out the $x$ are. And $b$ makes the line pass through the point of averages, $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$. Proving that this pair is the bottom of the valley takes calculus; the next cell checks it instead.

The formula lands at $a = 67.5$, $b = 712$, inside the grid square the loop found; the loop could only land on whole slopes and intercepts in steps of 100. The RMSE of the formula's line is the smallest any straight line can have on these points.

scikit-learn does the formula in one line. That is linear regression: draw the best straight line. Best means the smallest root mean squared error: the line that misses its points least.

scikit-learn is Python's library of methods that learn from data. You will use it in most weeks from now on, and every method in it works in the same three steps:

step code what it does make a model LinearRegression() a rule with numbers still to choose: here $y = a\,x + b$, with $a$ and $b$ unknown. Machine learning calls the numbers parameters fit it .fit(x, y) chooses the numbers from the data by making the RMSE as small as it can: for a line, the formula above. Machine learning calls that training ask it .predict(x) applies the rule to any x

Two different things happen in LinearRegression().fit(x, y). LinearRegression() makes the model: an empty one, with no $a$ and no $b$, because it has seen no data. .fit(x, y) gives it the data; the model chooses its two numbers and keeps them. fit also hands the fitted model back, which is why the two steps can sit on one line. In the next cell you do them one at a time, once, to see the difference.

x must be a table, because a fit can use several columns at once. supernovae["D(Mpc)"], one pair of brackets, is a single column. supernovae[["D(Mpc)"]], two pairs, is a table of one column, and that is what fit wants. y is the column to predict. LinearRegression came from the setup cell: from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression imports one method by name from a large library.

In the equations In scikit-learn $x$, $y$ the two arguments of .fit(x, y): x as a one-column table, y a column $a$, the slope model.coef_[0]: one slope for each column of x, so take the first $b$, the intercept model.intercept_ $y = a\,x + b$ at any $x$ model.predict(x) the $a$, $b$ with the smallest RMSE what .fit chooses, by the formula $b$ held at zero, so the line passes through the origin LinearRegression(fit_intercept=False) (section 3) $R^2$, how good the line is model.score(x, y) (section 3)

The underscore at the end of coef_ and intercept_ marks a number the fit chose.

Think. SN1992bp, at 309.5 Mpc, leaves at 23,646 km/s, and SN1992br, at 391.5 Mpc, at 26,318 km/s. Your line gives 24,349 km/s at 350 Mpc, between the two. Why is it reasonable to trust the line here? Would you trust it as much at 3,500 Mpc, far beyond the last supernova? The homework tests that.

The slope is the Hubble constant, and the physical model has no intercept. In 1929 Hubble wrote the line through these dots as a law:

$$v = H_0 \, d$$

where $v$ is a galaxy's speed, $d$ its distance, and $H_0$ the Hubble constant: how fast the universe is expanding now, in km/s per Mpc. Your slope, 67.5, is a measurement of $H_0$. The law has no intercept: at $d = 0$ it gives $v = 0$. The galaxy at zero distance is our own, and a galaxy cannot move away from itself, so in this model the line passes through the origin. Your free fit chose an intercept of 712 km/s because nothing told it not to; read literally, that would say our own galaxy is moving away from itself.

The free fit is still useful, as a check on the data: against speeds of tens of thousands of km/s, 712 is close to zero, so the supernovae are consistent with a line through the origin, as the law says.

Fit the line the physical model gives. When the physical model fixes a point on the line, the fit keeps it. In scikit-learn that is one argument, given when the model is made:

LinearRegression(fit_intercept=False).fit(x, y)

fit_intercept=False tells the model not to choose an intercept: $b$ is held at zero, and the fit chooses only $a$. Everything else is the same three steps, and .coef_[0] is still the slope. You will fit that line in section 4. First, how good is the free line?

R² is 0.978. The line's RMSE is about 15 percent of the flat line's, and R² works with the squares, so the line leaves about 2 percent of the flat line's squared miss. One thing to notice: the flat line's residuals are the distances of the speeds from their average, so its RMSE is the standard deviation of the speeds, the measure of spread from the probability week.

The residual plot of a good fit shows no pattern: the points lie on both sides of zero all the way across. A pattern is a tilt or a curve, and it means a straight line is the wrong shape, however high R² is. A second thing to look for is the scatter growing wider from one end to the other: the line is still the best straight line, but less sure at the wide end. Your plot shows no tilt or curve, a little widening toward the far end, and the two farthest supernovae below the line, a first hint of what you meet in the homework. Between 56.0 and 467.0 Mpc a straight line is a good description of these data. The universe is expanding, and you have measured how fast.

What R² looks like. R² is the square of the correlation coefficient $r$, a number between −1 and 1. The top row of the gallery shows clouds of points with $r$ from 1 (a perfect line going up) through 0 (no relation) to −1 (a perfect line going down). The middle row says that $r$ does not care how steep the line is: a perfect line gives 1 or −1 whatever its slope, and a flat line has no $r$ at all. The bottom row is the warning: in every one of those shapes $x$ and $y$ are clearly related, yet $r$ is 0, because the relation is not a straight line. R² cannot see that. The residual plot can.

A small number in an unfamiliar unit. The slope is in km/s per Mpc. One over it turns the unit upside down: Mpc per (km/s), which is megaparsec-seconds per kilometre, written Mpc·s/km. It is a time, written as a length divided by a speed. Three steps turn it into years, one unit at a time.

Step 1: a megaparsec is $3.0857 \times 10^{19}$ km. Multiply by that, and the Mpc cancels the Mpc while the km cancels the km, leaving seconds:

$$0.0148\ \frac{\text{Mpc}\cdot\text{s}}{\text{km}} \times 3.0857 \times 10^{19}\ \frac{\text{km}}{\text{Mpc}} = 4.57 \times 10^{17}\ \text{s}$$

Step 2: a year has $60 \times 60 \times 24 \times 365.25 = 31,557,600$ seconds. Divide by that, and the seconds cancel, leaving years:

$$\frac{4.57 \times 10^{17}\ \text{s}}{31,557,600\ \text{s/year}} = 1.45 \times 10^{10}\ \text{years}$$

Step 3: divide by a billion, $10^9$, to get 14.48 billion years.

Python writes such numbers with an e for "times ten to the": 3.0857e19 is $3.0857 \times 10^{19}$, 1e9 is a billion, and a result that prints as 4.57e+17 means $4.57 \times 10^{17}$. The next cell does the three steps.

Three ways to measure the Hubble constant, and they do not agree. The figure below, from Wendy Freedman's group, shows every published value from 2001 to 2019. Each dot is one measurement, its bar is the uncertainty the authors gave, and the shaded band joins the results of one method over the years. The three methods:

How to read the figure. In 2001 every bar was wide and they all overlapped, so the methods agreed. By 2016 the bars had shrunk, and the blue and the black no longer overlap: two careful methods give values 7 percent apart, more than their uncertainties allow. That disagreement is the Hubble tension. Either one method has an error nobody has found, or the model of the expansion that the CMB value relies on is missing something. It is one of the open questions of astronomy today, and Freedman explains it in this short video.

Why the published age is 13.8 billion years and not 1/H₀. Your calculation assumed that every galaxy has always moved at the speed it has today. That is the friend who drove 120 km at a steady 60 km/h. If the friend drove slowly at first and fast at the end, "two hours ago" is only an estimate.

The universe did both. For the first several billion years gravity slowed the expansion down. Since then it has been speeding up again, pushed by something astronomers call dark energy and do not yet understand. The published age comes from a model of that whole history, not from today's speed alone. The slowing and the speeding-up nearly cancel, which is why 1/H₀ lands within about 5 percent of 13.8: the right size, but not the exact age.

Where the second table comes from. Galaxies are not spread evenly through space: gravity gathers them into clusters, groups of tens to thousands of galaxies that move through space together. The clusters table holds 21 of them, from the same study as the supernovae, Wendy Freedman's Hubble Space Telescope Key Project (2001). Each row is one cluster: its speed away from us, measured from its redshift as before, and its distance, measured in a different way.

The second way to measure a distance. Every distance in this notebook needs a standard candle, an object whose true brightness is known, because how bright it looks then gives how far it is. The supernovae were one. The clusters use another: the spiral galaxies inside them. A spiral galaxy with more mass holds more stars, so it is brighter, and it also spins faster. The spin can be measured from the galaxy's light: one edge comes toward us and the other goes away, and the Doppler effect of section 1 widens its lines by an amount set by the speed of the spin. Faster spin means brighter galaxy: that is the Tully-Fisher relation, and with it the spin gives the true brightness, and the true brightness gives the distance. No supernova is needed. The table has the same two columns as supernovae, VCMB and D(Mpc), so the whole method of class applies unchanged. Look at it before you fit it: the setup cell loaded it as clusters.

A curve is one more column. The residuals of Your turn 10 arch, so the far supernovae want a curve, not a line. A line is $y = a\,x + b$: one column, $x$, with one slope. Give the fit a second column and it finds a second slope for it:

$$y = a_1\,x + a_2\,x_2 + b$$

Now make that second column the first one squared, $x_2 = x^2$. The rule becomes $y = a_1\,x + a_2\,x^2 + b$, and that is a curve: it bends upward if $a_2$ is positive and bends over if $a_2$ is negative. To scikit-learn nothing has changed. It is still choosing numbers to make the RMSE as small as it can, by the same least squares, and it does not care that one column was made from another. The fit is the same call with two columns inside the double brackets, [["D(Mpc)", "d2"]]; coef_ then holds two numbers, $a_1$ and $a_2$, one per column, and intercept_ is still $b$.

So the only new line is the one that makes the squared column. A table gets a new column when you assign to a name it does not have yet, with a whole old column on the right, as the earthquake week made region out of place:

table["new"] = table["old"] ** 2

Here the table is far_supernovae, the old column is D(Mpc) and the new one is d2.

docs.title: How old is the universe?¶
docs.text:
EPS 88 · PyEarth. Open your own copy on DataHub: click here.

In 1929 nobody knew whether the universe was standing still, shrinking or growing. The astronomer Edwin Hubble compared two measurements for nearby galaxies: how far away each one is, and how fast it is moving away from us. Plotted against each other, the points fell near a straight line: the farther a galaxy, the faster it leaves. That line means the universe is expanding, and its slope says how fast. Run the expansion backwards and every galaxy was once in the same place; the slope tells you how long ago.

Today you repeat Hubble's measurement with much better data: thirty-six exploding stars from a study led by the astronomer Wendy Freedman. You will find the best straight line through them three ways, by guessing, by trying every line and by a formula, then in one line of scikit-learn; check how good the line is; and turn its slope into an age for the universe. At home you try the same method on two more datasets, and find out where a straight line stops working.

Every place you write something opens with a pencil icon and the words Your turn, and is followed by a cell that already has the shape of the answer written in, with ... wherever your code goes. Replace every ..., run every cell so your answers and figures are saved in the file, then download this notebook itself — the .ipynb file — and upload it to Gradescope. Not a PDF: the marking reads your notebook, and a PDF cannot be read. In JupyterLab: File ▸ Download, or right-click the file in the left-hand panel and choose Download.

Two habits from the first minute. A cell runs when you press Shift+Enter, and the notebook remembers everything it has already run — so when something breaks and you cannot see why, Kernel → Restart Kernel and Run All Cells throws the memory away and rebuilds it from the top. That is never the wrong thing to do.

docs.title: What you'll be able to do¶
docs.text:
The science. Explain how a plot of speed against distance shows that the universe is expanding, why the best line through it should pass through the origin, and how its slope turns into an age.

The code. A straight line as two numbers, a and b · a residual, and the root mean squared error that sums them up · a loop that tries many lines · the least-squares formula · scikit-learn: LinearRegression().fit(x, y), .coef_[0], .intercept_, .predict(x), .score(x, y) and fit_intercept=False · a function that converts units.

Eleven places where you write something: seven in class, four at home. Each is headed Your turn, and the cell under it has the shape of the answer written in, with ... wherever your code goes and a comment beside each one saying what goes there. Early on the comment says how; later, once you have seen a thing done, it says only what.

The four questions of the class:

  1. How do we know the universe is expanding?
  2. How do we find the best straight line?
  3. What does the best line say about the universe, and how good is it?
  4. How old does that make the universe?

docs.title: Setup¶
docs.text: Run the next cell once. It loads the three small tables this week uses, all stored with the course: the supernovae for class, and two tables for the homework.

docs.title: 1. How do we know the universe is expanding?¶
docs.text:
To test whether the universe is expanding you need two measurements for each galaxy: how fast it is moving away from us, and how far away it is.

Speed comes from colour. You have heard the pitch of a siren drop as a fire engine passes you (listen to one). Sound is a wave, and the length of one wave, from crest to crest, is its wavelength. When the source moves away from you, each new crest starts from a little farther away, so the crests reach you farther apart: the wave arrives stretched. A longer sound wave has a lower pitch (the figure says frequency: fewer waves a second). This is the Doppler effect. In the picture, the car is moving to the right: the person it drives toward gets short waves and a high pitch, the person it leaves behind gets long waves and a low pitch.

Figure from The Physics Classroom.

Light is a wave too: when a galaxy moves away from us its light arrives with a longer wavelength, and a longer light wave is a redder colour. Astronomers call that a redshift.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 1¶
docs.text:
Does a galaxy that is farther away move away faster?

Why: if the universe is expanding, speed must grow with distance. A figure of one against the other is the test, and it is the figure Hubble drew.

  1. The figure. Draw the thirty-six supernovae as a scatter plot, as you did for earthquakes in the plotting week: distance across, speed up, and a label with units on each axis. The dots should climb from the lower left to the upper right.
  2. nearest and farthest: the smallest and the largest distance in the table. A result holds for the range of its data, so you will need this range later.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: nearest and farthest.

docs.title: 2. How do we find the best straight line?¶
docs.text:
A straight line is two numbers. Write $y$ for the thing up the page and $x$ for the thing across. Then every straight line is

$$y = a \, x + b$$

$a$ is the slope: how much $y$ grows for each unit of $x$. $b$ is the intercept: the value of $y$ where $x$ is zero, where the line crosses the vertical axis. Choose $a$ and $b$ and you have chosen the line. Finding the best line through a cloud of points means choosing the best pair. This section finds it for the supernovae three ways, each better than the last: by guessing, by trying every pair, and by a formula. Then scikit-learn does it in one line.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 2¶
docs.text:
Guess the line.

Why: before any formula, see what a slope and an intercept do to a line, and how far a guess can be from the data. Four guesses of your own, drawn on the dots, show it.

  1. draw_line(a, b): a function that draws the line $y = a\,x + b$ from 0 to 500 Mpc onto whatever figure is open. Its body is one drawing call: a line needs only its two end points, at $x = 0$ and $x = 500$, which line_x holds, and its two speeds are a * line_x + b. The label names the pair, so the legend tells the lines apart.
  2. guesses: four pairs of your own, each a list [a, b]. From Your turn 1, the speeds reach about 30,000 km/s at 470 Mpc, so slopes between 40 and 100 are worth trying, and intercepts between −5,000 and 5,000.
  3. The figure: the supernovae as dots, then the loop calls your function once per pair, so all four lines land on the same dots. Which looks best? Which is too flat, and which starts in the wrong place?

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: draw_line and guesses.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 3¶
docs.text:
Try every line.

Why: the best line is the one with the smallest RMSE. A loop inside a loop can try every whole slope from 50 to 90 and every intercept from −3,000 to 3,000 in steps of 100, and keep three lists: each RMSE, and the a and b that made it. That is 2,501 lines in a second, and the smallest RMSE in the list is the best line.

  1. Inside the loops: for each b and each a, the residuals and the RMSE, as in the cell above, then append the RMSE to rmses, and a and b to slopes and intercepts, so that the three lists line up.
  2. lowest, where, best_a and best_b: the smallest RMSE with np.min, its position in rmses with np.argmin, and the slope and intercept at that same position in the other two lists, as you read one list by the position found in another in the first week.
  3. The rest is given: the 2,501 RMSEs reshaped into a grid, one row per intercept, and drawn as a picture, as the elevation week drew a grid, with your guesses as dots and the best pair as a star.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: rmse_grid, lowest, best_a and best_b.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 4¶
docs.text:
The formula, by hand.

Why: a formula you have applied once is one you can trust, and the loop gives you the answer to check it against.

  1. x_from_mean and y_from_mean: how far each distance is from the average distance, and each speed from the average speed. One line each, on the whole column.
  2. a_by_hand: the top of the formula over its bottom: the two columns multiplied and summed, over the squared distances-from-mean summed.
  3. b_by_hand: the average speed minus a_by_hand times the average distance.

The print sets your two numbers beside best_a and best_b, the best pair the loop found in Your turn 3.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: a_by_hand and b_by_hand.

docs.title: 3. What does the best line say about the universe, and how good is it?¶
docs.text: Section 2 was the method, and you now know what scikit-learn does when it fits a line. From here on the notebook uses it directly and reads the science off the line: its slope is a measurement, its intercept is fixed by the physical model, and its residuals say how far to trust it.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 5¶
docs.text:
Fit the supernovae with scikit-learn, and use the line.

Why: this is the call you will make in every later week. Its two numbers should match the formula (a_by_hand, b_by_hand) and the loop (best_a, best_b), and a fitted line can give a speed at a distance where nothing was measured.

  1. model: the first two lines make the empty model and print it; then fit it: distance as x, as a one-column table, and speed as y.
  2. slope and intercept: the two numbers of the line, read from the model.
  3. line_speed: the line's speed at each supernova's distance, from model.predict.
  4. speed_350: the speed the rule gives a galaxy 350 Mpc away: speed = slope × 350 + intercept. No supernova is at that distance, but it is inside the range of the table.
  5. The figure, three things on it: the supernovae as dots, the line on top in black, and your prediction as one red cross at distance 350. The line should run through the middle of the dots, and the cross should sit on it. Remember the difference: plt.scatter draws one dot per row and joins nothing; plt.plot joins its points in order into a line. Every value of line_speed lies on the same straight line, so the order of the rows does not matter.

Two errors to expect: Expected a 2-dimensional container means the distance needs its second pair of brackets; doesn't define __round__ means the slope needs its [0].

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: model, slope, intercept, line_speed and speed_350.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 6¶
docs.text:
How well does the line fit the supernovae?

Why: a line can be the best one and still be the wrong shape for its data. Two things tell you: a picture, the residual plot, the residuals drawn against distance; and one number, R².

R² compares your line with the simplest line there is, a flat one at the average speed, which ignores distance altogether:

$$R^2 = 1 - \left(\frac{\text{RMSE of the fitted line}}{\text{RMSE of the flat line}}\right)^2$$

It is 1 when every point sits on the line, and near 0 when the line does no better than the average. The flat line is the yardstick; it has no R² of its own here.

  1. residuals: the real speed minus line_speed, one for each supernova.
  2. The figure: the residuals against distance, as dots, with a horizontal line at zero to measure from. plt.axhline(0) draws one.
  3. line_rmse: the RMSE of the fitted line, as in section 2.
  4. flat_rmse: the RMSE of a flat line at the average speed: the residuals of that line are each speed minus the average speed.
  5. r_squared: by the equation, from the two RMSEs. The last line asks scikit-learn for the same number with model.score(x, y), which takes the same two things the fit was given.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: residuals, line_rmse, flat_rmse and r_squared.

docs.title: 4. How old does that make the universe?¶
docs.text:
This section uses slope from Your turn 5; run that cell again if you restarted.

A friend arrives at your door and says: "I drove 120 km at 60 km/h." You know when your friend left: 120 divided by 60, two hours ago. Time is distance divided by speed. The same works for a galaxy. If it has always moved at the speed it has today, the time since it was right here is

$$t = \frac{d}{v}$$

Hubble's law says $v = H_0 d$. Put that in, and the distance cancels:

$$t = \frac{d}{H_0 \, d} = \frac{1}{H_0}$$

The same time for every galaxy, near or far: they all set out together. So one over the slope is an age for the universe.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 7¶
docs.text:
Write the conversion once, as a function, and use it on both lines.

Why: you now have two lines, and the homework brings more. A function does the three steps in one call, for any slope.

  1. age_of_universe(hubble_constant): it takes a Hubble constant in km/s per Mpc and returns one over it, in billions of years. Its body is the three steps of the cell above, with hubble_constant in place of slope, and it ends with return, as your functions in the functions week did. The two constants are written again inside the function, so that it needs nothing from outside.
  2. age: call the function on your slope, the free line's.
  3. origin_model and H0_origin: fit the line through the origin, with fit_intercept=False as section 3 showed, and read its slope.
  4. age_origin: call the function on H0_origin.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: age_of_universe, age, origin_model, H0_origin and age_origin.

docs.title: The question, answered¶
docs.text: About 14 billion years. One over the slope of the best straight line through thirty-six supernovae gives 13.84 billion years when the line starts at zero, as Hubble's law says it must. The published age, from a model of the whole expansion, is 13.8 billion years. The close agreement is partly luck: 1/H₀ is a time of the right size, not the exact age, because the expansion has not been steady. The free line gave 14.48, and the Planck value of H₀ gives 14.51.

docs.title: The science¶
docs.text:
How old is the universe? A slope can be an age: the slope of speed against distance is how fast the universe expands, and one over it is a time. The best straight line has the smallest total of squared residuals. The physical model can also fix a point on it: Hubble's law has no intercept, so the line is fitted through the origin. Before trusting a line, draw it on its data and look at what it misses: R² is one number, and the residual plot shows whether there is a pattern.

  • Residual. A residual is the real value minus the line's value.
  • Linear regression. Draw the best straight line. Best means the smallest root mean squared error: the line that misses its points least.
  • Fit through the origin. When the physical model fixes a point on the line, the fit keeps it.

docs.text: Function What it does Python for x in things: a loop — here, over every slope to try list.append(x) add x to the end of a list — here, one RMSE per slope round(x, 1) trim a long decimal — 9.1 rather than sixteen digits def name(a, b): a function — here, a unit conversion you will use again NumPy np.min(values) the smallest value — here, the smallest RMSE np.argmin(values) the position of the smallest value — here, where the smallest RMSE sits, to read its slope and intercept from the other two lists Matplotlib plt.axhline(y) a horizontal line at y, to mark zero on a residual plot plt.scatter(x, y) one dot for each row — the data plt.plot(x, y) join points with a line — here, the fitted line drawn on its data plt.xlabel / ylabel / title / show label it, then draw it scikit-learn LinearRegression().fit(x, y) find the straight line with the smallest total of squared residuals model.coef_[0] the slope of the fitted line model.intercept_ where the fitted line crosses zero model.predict(x) what the fitted line says y should be at each x model.score(x, y) R² — the share of a flat line's squared residuals that the fitted line removes; 1 is a perfect fit LinearRegression(fit_intercept=False) the same fit, forced to pass through (0, 0)

from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# house style, set once, so every plot cell below holds only what matters

                     "axes.grid": True, "grid.alpha": 0.3, "axes.axisbelow": True})

CACHE = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AI4EPS/EPS88_PyEarth/main/data"

# 36 Type Ia supernovae (Freedman and colleagues, 2001): the three columns to keep are name, speed and distance
supernovae = pd.read_csv(CACHE + "/week06_supernovae.csv")[["Supernova", "VCMB", "D(Mpc)"]]

# For the homework. 21 clusters of galaxies from the same study, with distances measured another way:

# and supernovae much farther away (Betoule and colleagues, 2014): redshift, speed and distance

How do we know how long the waves were when they left? Hydrogen absorbs light at a few exact wavelengths (measured in nanometres, billionths of a metre), and they show as dark lines in the light of a star: the same pattern everywhere in the universe, like a barcode. In the light of a galaxy that is moving away, the whole barcode sits at longer wavelengths, toward the red end of the rainbow; in the light of one moving toward us, toward the blue:

Figures from A-level Physics Tutor.

The size of the shift gives the speed: for speeds well below light's, each wavelength grows by the fraction (the galaxy's speed) / (the speed of light). The fastest galaxy in today's table is leaving at 30,253 km/s, about a tenth of the speed of light, so every one of its lines sits a tenth farther along: hydrogen's red line, at 656 nanometres in a laboratory, arrives at 722. The far-red lines move more than the violet ones, because each one moves by the same fraction of itself: the barcode is stretched, not slid.

Distance comes from brightness. A lamp looks dimmer the farther away it is. So if you know how bright a lamp really is, how bright it looks tells you its distance. Astronomers call such a lamp a standard candle, and a Type Ia supernova is one. It is the explosion of a white dwarf, the small, dense remains of a star, after it has gained matter from a companion star or merged with another white dwarf. These explosions are so alike that astronomers can work out how bright each one really was at its peak. They are also bright enough to be seen in galaxies more than a billion light-years away. Distances that large are measured in megaparsecs (Mpc). One megaparsec is 3.26 million light-years: light, the fastest thing there is, takes 3.26 million years to cross it.

Each row of supernovae is one supernova. VCMB is the speed of its galaxy away from us, in km/s, with our own motion taken out: the CMB in the name is the cosmic microwave background, the oldest light in the universe, which astronomers use as the fixed background to measure speeds against. D(Mpc) is its distance in megaparsecs. That column name has brackets in it, so it always goes in quotes: supernovae["D(Mpc)"].

Farther means faster, and the points fall close to a straight line. Every distant galaxy is moving away from us, and a galaxy twice as far leaves about twice as fast. That is what an expanding universe looks like from inside it. Think of dots drawn on a rubber band, one centimetre apart, and stretch the band to one and a half times its length in one second. Seen from your dot, the dot that was 1 cm away is now at 1.5 cm: it moved 0.5 cm. The dot that was 4 cm away is now at 6 cm: it moved 2 cm, in the same second, so four times as far means four times as fast. Stand on any other dot and you see the same thing. No dot is the centre; the band is simply stretching everywhere.

How fast the universe is expanding is the slope of that line: how many km/s of speed each megaparsec of distance adds. So the measurement you need is the slope of the best straight line through these dots, and section 2 teaches how to find it.

Judging by eye is not enough. Two guesses that both look close cannot be told apart by looking. To choose between them you need a number that says how badly a line misses its points.

A residual is the real value minus the line's value.

$$\text{residual} = \text{real value} - \text{the line's value}$$

Take the first supernova in the table, SN1990O, 134.7 Mpc away at 9,065 km/s, and a reasonable guess, $a = 72$ and $b = 300$. The line gives it $72 \times 134.7 + 300 = 9,998$ km/s. Its residual for that line is $9,065 - 9,998 = -933$ km/s: the point sits that far below the line. A point above the line has a positive residual.

To judge a whole line with one number, use the root mean squared error, RMSE. A line has thirty-six residuals. Square each one, so that misses above and below the line cannot cancel; take the mean of the squares; take the square root, which brings the number back to km/s:

$$\text{RMSE} = \sqrt{\text{mean of the squared residuals}}$$

The RMSE is the typical miss of the line, in the units of the data. Try it on three residuals, 2, −2 and 1. Added as they are they give 1, as if the line hardly missed. Their squares are 4, 4 and 1, the mean is 3, and the square root of 3 is 1.7. In Python the square root is a power of one half: (mean) ** 0.5. Squaring makes a line care most about its worst misses; the number a fit tries to make small is also called its loss. The next cell scores your four guesses, and the example line.

The picture is a valley. Every pair in the dark band is a good line, and the band runs diagonally: a steeper line can be made nearly as good by starting it lower. The lowest point is $a = 67$, $b = 800$, with an RMSE of 943 km/s. Finding it this way is called least squares: the line with the smallest RMSE is the line with the smallest total of squared residuals, the same thing.

Trying every pair works, but it is slow and it only finds pairs on the grid. For a straight line there is a formula that goes to the bottom of the valley directly.

The formula. Call the distances $x_1, \ldots, x_n$ and the speeds $y_1, \ldots, y_n$, with $n = 36$, and let $\bar{x}$ and $\bar{y}$ be their averages. The $a$ and $b$ with the smallest RMSE are

$$a = \frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}, \qquad b = \bar{y} - a\,\bar{x}$$

The top of $a$ adds up, over the points, how far each one is from the average in $x$ times how far it is in $y$: positive when the two go together. The bottom is how spread out the $x$ are. And $b$ makes the line pass through the point of averages, $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$. Proving that this pair is the bottom of the valley takes calculus; the next cell checks it instead.

The formula lands at $a = 67.5$, $b = 712$, inside the grid square the loop found; the loop could only land on whole slopes and intercepts in steps of 100. The RMSE of the formula's line is the smallest any straight line can have on these points.

scikit-learn does the formula in one line. That is linear regression: draw the best straight line. Best means the smallest root mean squared error: the line that misses its points least.

scikit-learn is Python's library of methods that learn from data. You will use it in most weeks from now on, and every method in it works in the same three steps:

step code what it does make a model LinearRegression() a rule with numbers still to choose: here $y = a\,x + b$, with $a$ and $b$ unknown. Machine learning calls the numbers parameters fit it .fit(x, y) chooses the numbers from the data by making the RMSE as small as it can: for a line, the formula above. Machine learning calls that training ask it .predict(x) applies the rule to any x

Two different things happen in LinearRegression().fit(x, y). LinearRegression() makes the model: an empty one, with no $a$ and no $b$, because it has seen no data. .fit(x, y) gives it the data; the model chooses its two numbers and keeps them. fit also hands the fitted model back, which is why the two steps can sit on one line. In the next cell you do them one at a time, once, to see the difference.

x must be a table, because a fit can use several columns at once. supernovae["D(Mpc)"], one pair of brackets, is a single column. supernovae[["D(Mpc)"]], two pairs, is a table of one column, and that is what fit wants. y is the column to predict. LinearRegression came from the setup cell: from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression imports one method by name from a large library.

In the equations In scikit-learn $x$, $y$ the two arguments of .fit(x, y): x as a one-column table, y a column $a$, the slope model.coef_[0]: one slope for each column of x, so take the first $b$, the intercept model.intercept_ $y = a\,x + b$ at any $x$ model.predict(x) the $a$, $b$ with the smallest RMSE what .fit chooses, by the formula $b$ held at zero, so the line passes through the origin LinearRegression(fit_intercept=False) (section 3) $R^2$, how good the line is model.score(x, y) (section 3)

The underscore at the end of coef_ and intercept_ marks a number the fit chose.

Think. SN1992bp, at 309.5 Mpc, leaves at 23,646 km/s, and SN1992br, at 391.5 Mpc, at 26,318 km/s. Your line gives 24,349 km/s at 350 Mpc, between the two. Why is it reasonable to trust the line here? Would you trust it as much at 3,500 Mpc, far beyond the last supernova? The homework tests that.

The slope is the Hubble constant, and the physical model has no intercept. In 1929 Hubble wrote the line through these dots as a law:

$$v = H_0 \, d$$

where $v$ is a galaxy's speed, $d$ its distance, and $H_0$ the Hubble constant: how fast the universe is expanding now, in km/s per Mpc. Your slope, 67.5, is a measurement of $H_0$. The law has no intercept: at $d = 0$ it gives $v = 0$. The galaxy at zero distance is our own, and a galaxy cannot move away from itself, so in this model the line passes through the origin. Your free fit chose an intercept of 712 km/s because nothing told it not to; read literally, that would say our own galaxy is moving away from itself.

The free fit is still useful, as a check on the data: against speeds of tens of thousands of km/s, 712 is close to zero, so the supernovae are consistent with a line through the origin, as the law says.

Fit the line the physical model gives. When the physical model fixes a point on the line, the fit keeps it. In scikit-learn that is one argument, given when the model is made:

LinearRegression(fit_intercept=False).fit(x, y)

fit_intercept=False tells the model not to choose an intercept: $b$ is held at zero, and the fit chooses only $a$. Everything else is the same three steps, and .coef_[0] is still the slope. You will fit that line in section 4. First, how good is the free line?

R² is 0.978. The line's RMSE is about 15 percent of the flat line's, and R² works with the squares, so the line leaves about 2 percent of the flat line's squared miss. One thing to notice: the flat line's residuals are the distances of the speeds from their average, so its RMSE is the standard deviation of the speeds, the measure of spread from the probability week.

The residual plot of a good fit shows no pattern: the points lie on both sides of zero all the way across. A pattern is a tilt or a curve, and it means a straight line is the wrong shape, however high R² is. A second thing to look for is the scatter growing wider from one end to the other: the line is still the best straight line, but less sure at the wide end. Your plot shows no tilt or curve, a little widening toward the far end, and the two farthest supernovae below the line, a first hint of what you meet in the homework. Between 56.0 and 467.0 Mpc a straight line is a good description of these data. The universe is expanding, and you have measured how fast.

What R² looks like. R² is the square of the correlation coefficient $r$, a number between −1 and 1. The top row of the gallery shows clouds of points with $r$ from 1 (a perfect line going up) through 0 (no relation) to −1 (a perfect line going down). The middle row says that $r$ does not care how steep the line is: a perfect line gives 1 or −1 whatever its slope, and a flat line has no $r$ at all. The bottom row is the warning: in every one of those shapes $x$ and $y$ are clearly related, yet $r$ is 0, because the relation is not a straight line. R² cannot see that. The residual plot can.

A small number in an unfamiliar unit. The slope is in km/s per Mpc. One over it turns the unit upside down: Mpc per (km/s), which is megaparsec-seconds per kilometre, written Mpc·s/km. It is a time, written as a length divided by a speed. Three steps turn it into years, one unit at a time.

Step 1: a megaparsec is $3.0857 \times 10^{19}$ km. Multiply by that, and the Mpc cancels the Mpc while the km cancels the km, leaving seconds:

$$0.0148\ \frac{\text{Mpc}\cdot\text{s}}{\text{km}} \times 3.0857 \times 10^{19}\ \frac{\text{km}}{\text{Mpc}} = 4.57 \times 10^{17}\ \text{s}$$

Step 2: a year has $60 \times 60 \times 24 \times 365.25 = 31,557,600$ seconds. Divide by that, and the seconds cancel, leaving years:

$$\frac{4.57 \times 10^{17}\ \text{s}}{31,557,600\ \text{s/year}} = 1.45 \times 10^{10}\ \text{years}$$

Step 3: divide by a billion, $10^9$, to get 14.48 billion years.

Python writes such numbers with an e for "times ten to the": 3.0857e19 is $3.0857 \times 10^{19}$, 1e9 is a billion, and a result that prints as 4.57e+17 means $4.57 \times 10^{17}$. The next cell does the three steps.

def age_of_universe(hubble_constant):
    """one over a Hubble constant in km/s per Mpc, as an age in billions of years"""
    MPC_IN_KM = 3.0857e+19  # kilometres in one megaparsec
    SECONDS_PER_YEAR = 60 * 60 * 24 * 365.25
    seconds = (1 / hubble_constant) * MPC_IN_KM
    years = seconds / SECONDS_PER_YEAR
    return years / 1e9

Three ways to measure the Hubble constant, and they do not agree. The figure below, from Wendy Freedman's group, shows every published value from 2001 to 2019. Each dot is one measurement, its bar is the uncertainty the authors gave, and the shaded band joins the results of one method over the years. The three methods:

method colour how it works value today Cepheids blue stars that pulse at a rate set by their true brightness: a standard candle, like the supernovae, so a distance and a speed, as in this notebook about 74 CMB black the cosmic microwave background, the oldest light in the universe, released 380,000 years after the start: the pattern of its hot and cold spots, put through a model of the expansion, gives H₀. The Planck value, 67.4, is the last black dot about 67 TRGB red the tip of the red giant branch: the brightest red giant stars all have the same true brightness, so they are a second standard candle. Figure from Freedman et al. (2019), arXiv:1907.05922.

How to read the figure. In 2001 every bar was wide and they all overlapped, so the methods agreed. By 2016 the bars had shrunk, and the blue and the black no longer overlap: two careful methods give values 7 percent apart, more than their uncertainties allow. That disagreement is the Hubble tension. Either one method has an error nobody has found, or the model of the expansion that the CMB value relies on is missing something. It is one of the open questions of astronomy today, and Freedman explains it in this short video.

Why the published age is 13.8 billion years and not 1/H₀. Your calculation assumed that every galaxy has always moved at the speed it has today. That is the friend who drove 120 km at a steady 60 km/h. If the friend drove slowly at first and fast at the end, "two hours ago" is only an estimate.

The universe did both. For the first several billion years gravity slowed the expansion down. Since then it has been speeding up again, pushed by something astronomers call dark energy and do not yet understand. The published age comes from a model of that whole history, not from today's speed alone. The slowing and the speeding-up nearly cancel, which is why 1/H₀ lands within about 5 percent of 13.8: the right size, but not the exact age.

Where the second table comes from. Galaxies are not spread evenly through space: gravity gathers them into clusters, groups of tens to thousands of galaxies that move through space together. The clusters table holds 21 of them, from the same study as the supernovae, Wendy Freedman's Hubble Space Telescope Key Project (2001). Each row is one cluster: its speed away from us, measured from its redshift as before, and its distance, measured in a different way.

The second way to measure a distance. Every distance in this notebook needs a standard candle, an object whose true brightness is known, because how bright it looks then gives how far it is. The supernovae were one. The clusters use another: the spiral galaxies inside them. A spiral galaxy with more mass holds more stars, so it is brighter, and it also spins faster. The spin can be measured from the galaxy's light: one edge comes toward us and the other goes away, and the Doppler effect of section 1 widens its lines by an amount set by the speed of the spin. Faster spin means brighter galaxy: that is the Tully-Fisher relation, and with it the spin gives the true brightness, and the true brightness gives the distance. No supernova is needed. The table has the same two columns as supernovae, VCMB and D(Mpc), so the whole method of class applies unchanged. Look at it before you fit it: the setup cell loaded it as clusters.

What the numbers mean. The clusters give a Hubble constant of 76.0 km/s per Mpc and an age of 12.87 billion years; the supernovae gave 70.7 and 13.84. First, is the clusters' line a good fit? It misses by 357 km/s where the class line missed by 998, but the clusters are nearer and slower, averaging 4,289 km/s against 12,745: as a share of the typical speed the two misses are alike, about 8 percent against 8, and R² agrees, 0.967 against 0.976. The residual plot shows no pattern. So the gap of about 5 km/s per Mpc, or about a billion years, is not a bad fit on either side. Two things feed it. A galaxy's own motion of a few hundred km/s matters more when the expansion carries it at only 1,088 to 8,930 km/s. And each method has its own way of deciding how bright its objects really are; an error there moves every distance in the table together. If one method put every distance 10 percent too large, its slope would come out about 10 percent too small and its age about 10 percent too large. The study these tables come from reports 71 km/s per Mpc for both methods, after corrections that this table does not carry, so the gap here is not a difference between the methods. These two tables cannot say which value is right. A distance measured both ways for the same galaxies would.

Twenty times farther. far_supernovae comes from a later study that reaches 9,212 Mpc, about 20 times the farthest supernova in supernovae. Each row is an average over many supernovae at about the same distance. The table has three columns: z, the redshift, the fraction by which the wavelengths are stretched, which is what astronomers measure; VCMB, that redshift turned into a speed with the formula that keeps every speed below the speed of light (the simple rule of section 1 holds only for speeds well below it); and D(Mpc), the distance.

Here is the study's own figure: 740 supernovae from four surveys, on the astronomers' axes, $z$ and $\mu$ (a measure of distance). The $z$ axis is a log axis, as in the plotting week, and on it the points look like a perfect straight line. Keep that in mind: a log axis can hide a curve.

Figure from Betoule et al. (2014), Astronomy and Astrophysics 568, A22.

What the numbers mean. Inside the range of the class data, the crowded lower-left corner of the figure, the far supernovae lie within about 15 percent of the line, 12 of 14 a little below it. Beyond that range they fall farther and farther below, and at the farthest one the line gives 651,016 km/s where the table has 204,469: 3.2 times too fast, and more than twice the speed of light, which nothing can reach. The line was fitted to supernovae between 56.0 and 467.0 Mpc, and there it fits well. Nothing in the fit said it would hold 20 times farther out, and it does not. A fitted line describes the range of its data; using it far outside that range is extrapolation, and it is a guess. How large the miss is depends on how speed and distance are worked out that far away. With the speed worked out from the redshift and the distance from the brightness, as in this table, a straight line fails. The class result is not wrong: it is a result about the nearby universe.

What the numbers mean. The new line has an R² of 0.921, which sounds like a good fit, and a slope of 24.5 km/s per Mpc, which would make the universe 40.0 billion years old. The residuals show what R² hides, as the bottom row of the correlation gallery warned: the nearest 15 rows all sit below the line (they overlap at the left edge of the panel), the next 14 sit above it, and the last 2 below again. That is an arch, not noise. The data curve, so no straight line can describe them, and a slope taken from one means little. The next part fits the curve, the way astronomers do.

A curve is one more column. The residuals of Your turn 10 arch, so the far supernovae want a curve, not a line. A line is $y = a\,x + b$: one column, $x$, with one slope. Give the fit a second column and it finds a second slope for it:

$$y = a_1\,x + a_2\,x_2 + b$$

Now make that second column the first one squared, $x_2 = x^2$. The rule becomes $y = a_1\,x + a_2\,x^2 + b$, and that is a curve: it bends upward if $a_2$ is positive and bends over if $a_2$ is negative. To scikit-learn nothing has changed. It is still choosing numbers to make the RMSE as small as it can, by the same least squares, and it does not care that one column was made from another. The fit is the same call with two columns inside the double brackets, [["D(Mpc)", "d2"]]; coef_ then holds two numbers, $a_1$ and $a_2$, one per column, and intercept_ is still $b$.

So the only new line is the one that makes the squared column. A table gets a new column when you assign to a name it does not have yet, with a whole old column on the right, as the earthquake week made region out of place:

table["new"] = table["old"] ** 2

Here the table is far_supernovae, the old column is D(Mpc) and the new one is d2.

✓ Your turn 11 — the curve misses by 4,971 km/s, against the line's 17,140, with R² 0.993

What the numbers mean. The curve is much better and still not right. Its RMSE is 4,971 km/s against the line's 17,140, and R² rises from 0.921 to 0.993. But the residual plot still has a shape, 12 below, then 14 above, then below again: a curve with one bend is not quite the shape of these data either.

And the curve's numbers have no physical meaning. Its $a_2$ is negative, so the curve bends over and would start to fall beyond about 8,300 Mpc, as if the farthest galaxies slowed down. That is a property of the columns, not of the universe. The speed in VCMB was worked out from the redshift by a formula that can never exceed the speed of light, while the distance keeps growing, so any curve through these points must flatten, in a universe that is speeding up or in one that is slowing down. The bend cannot tell the two apart. Astronomers fit distance against the redshift itself, the thing the spectrograph measures, with a $z^2$ term like your d2, and there the size of the bend measures whether the expansion is slowing down or speeding up today. In 1998 two teams fitted supernovae like these and found it speeding up, the discovery that won the 2011 Nobel prize; the cause was named dark energy. It is also why the published age is so close to 1/H₀: with gravity alone the universe would be only two thirds of that, about 9.2 billion years old, and the speeding-up since has nearly cancelled the early slowing, as section 4 said.

docs.title: How old is the universe?¶
docs.text:
EPS 88 · PyEarth. Open your own copy on DataHub: click here.

In 1929 nobody knew whether the universe was standing still, shrinking or growing. The astronomer Edwin Hubble compared two measurements for nearby galaxies: how far away each one is, and how fast it is moving away from us. Plotted against each other, the points fell near a straight line: the farther a galaxy, the faster it leaves. That line means the universe is expanding, and its slope says how fast. Run the expansion backwards and every galaxy was once in the same place; the slope tells you how long ago.

Today you repeat Hubble's measurement with much better data: thirty-six exploding stars from a study led by the astronomer Wendy Freedman. You will find the best straight line through them three ways, by guessing, by trying every line and by a formula, then in one line of scikit-learn; check how good the line is; and turn its slope into an age for the universe. At home you try the same method on two more datasets, and find out where a straight line stops working.

Every place you write something opens with a pencil icon and the words Your turn, and is followed by a cell that already has the shape of the answer written in, with ... wherever your code goes. Replace every ..., run every cell so your answers and figures are saved in the file, then download this notebook itself — the .ipynb file — and upload it to Gradescope. Not a PDF: the marking reads your notebook, and a PDF cannot be read. In JupyterLab: File ▸ Download, or right-click the file in the left-hand panel and choose Download.

Two habits from the first minute. A cell runs when you press Shift+Enter, and the notebook remembers everything it has already run — so when something breaks and you cannot see why, Kernel → Restart Kernel and Run All Cells throws the memory away and rebuilds it from the top. That is never the wrong thing to do.

docs.text:
The science. Explain how a plot of speed against distance shows that the universe is expanding, why the best line through it should pass through the origin, and how its slope turns into an age.

The code. A straight line as two numbers, a and b · a residual, and the root mean squared error that sums them up · a loop that tries many lines · the least-squares formula · scikit-learn: LinearRegression().fit(x, y), .coef_[0], .intercept_, .predict(x), .score(x, y) and fit_intercept=False · a function that converts units.

Early on the comment says how; later, once you have seen a thing done, it says only what.

The four questions of the class:

  1. How do we know the universe is expanding?
  2. How do we find the best straight line?

docs.title: 1. How do we know the universe is expanding?¶
docs.text:
To test whether the universe is expanding you need two measurements for each galaxy: how fast it is moving away from us, and how far away it is.

Speed comes from colour. You have heard the pitch of a siren drop as a fire engine passes you (listen to one). Sound is a wave, and the length of one wave, from crest to crest, is its wavelength. When the source moves away from you, each new crest starts from a little farther away, so the crests reach you farther apart: the wave arrives stretched. A longer sound wave has a lower pitch (the figure says frequency: fewer waves a second). This is the Doppler effect. In the picture, the car is moving to the right: the person it drives toward gets short waves and a high pitch, the person it leaves behind gets long waves and a low pitch.

Figure from The Physics Classroom.

Light is a wave too: when a galaxy moves away from us its light arrives with a longer wavelength, and a longer light wave is a redder colour. Astronomers call that a redshift.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 1¶
docs.text:
Does a galaxy that is farther away move away faster?

Why: if the universe is expanding, speed must grow with distance. A figure of one against the other is the test, and it is the figure Hubble drew.

  1. The figure. Draw the thirty-six supernovae as a scatter plot, as you did for earthquakes in the plotting week: distance across, speed up, and a label with units on each axis. The dots should climb from the lower left to the upper right.
  2. nearest and farthest: the smallest and the largest distance in the table. A result holds for the range of its data, so you will need this range later.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: nearest and farthest.

docs.title: 2. How do we find the best straight line?¶
docs.text:
A straight line is two numbers. Write $y$ for the thing up the page and $x$ for the thing across. Then every straight line is

$$y = a \, x + b$$

$a$ is the slope: how much $y$ grows for each unit of $x$. $b$ is the intercept: the value of $y$ where $x$ is zero, where the line crosses the vertical axis. Choose $a$ and $b$ and you have chosen the line. Finding the best line through a cloud of points means choosing the best pair. This section finds it for the supernovae three ways, each better than the last: by guessing, by trying every pair, and by a formula. Then scikit-learn does it in one line.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 2¶
docs.text:
Guess the line.

Why: before any formula, see what a slope and an intercept do to a line, and how far a guess can be from the data. Four guesses of your own, drawn on the dots, show it.

  1. draw_line(a, b): a function that draws the line $y = a\,x + b$ from 0 to 500 Mpc onto whatever figure is open. Its body is one drawing call: a line needs only its two end points, at $x = 0$ and $x = 500$, which line_x holds, and its two speeds are a * line_x + b. The label names the pair, so the legend tells the lines apart.
  2. guesses: four pairs of your own, each a list [a, b]. From Your turn 1, the speeds reach about 30,000 km/s at 470 Mpc, so slopes between 40 and 100 are worth trying, and intercepts between −5,000 and 5,000.
  3. The figure: the supernovae as dots, then the loop calls your function once per pair, so all four lines land on the same dots. Which looks best? Which is too flat, and which starts in the wrong place?

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: draw_line and guesses.

docs.text:
Try every line.

Why: the best line is the one with the smallest RMSE. A loop inside a loop can try every whole slope from 50 to 90 and every intercept from −3,000 to 3,000 in steps of 100, and keep three lists: each RMSE, and the a and b that made it. That is 2,501 lines in a second, and the smallest RMSE in the list is the best line.

  1. Inside the loops: for each b and each a, the residuals and the RMSE, as in the cell above, then append the RMSE to rmses, and a and b to slopes and intercepts, so that the three lists line up.
  2. lowest, where, best_a and best_b: the smallest RMSE with np.min, its position in rmses with np.argmin, and the slope and intercept at that same position in the other two lists, as you read one list by the position found in another in the first week.
  3. The rest is given: the 2,501 RMSEs reshaped into a grid, one row per intercept, and drawn as a picture, as the elevation week drew a grid, with your guesses as dots and the best pair as a star.

docs.text:

Why: a formula you have applied once is one you can trust, and the loop gives you the answer to check it against.

  1. x_from_mean and y_from_mean: how far each distance is from the average distance, and each speed from the average speed. One line each, on the whole column.
  2. a_by_hand: the top of the formula over its bottom: the two columns multiplied and summed, over the squared distances-from-mean summed.
  3. b_by_hand: the average speed minus a_by_hand times the average distance.

The print sets your two numbers beside best_a and best_b, the best pair the loop found in Your turn 3.

docs.title: 3. What does the best line say about the universe, and how good is it?¶
docs.text: Section 2 was the method, and you now know what scikit-learn does when it fits a line. From here on the notebook uses it directly and reads the science off the line: its slope is a measurement, its intercept is fixed by the physical model, and its residuals say how far to trust it.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 5¶
docs.text:
Fit the supernovae with scikit-learn, and use the line.

Why: this is the call you will make in every later week. Its two numbers should match the formula (a_by_hand, b_by_hand) and the loop (best_a, best_b), and a fitted line can give a speed at a distance where nothing was measured.

  1. model: the first two lines make the empty model and print it; then fit it: distance as x, as a one-column table, and speed as y.
  2. slope and intercept: the two numbers of the line, read from the model.
  3. line_speed: the line's speed at each supernova's distance, from model.predict.
  4. speed_350: the speed the rule gives a galaxy 350 Mpc away: speed = slope × 350 + intercept. No supernova is at that distance, but it is inside the range of the table.
  5. The figure, three things on it: the supernovae as dots, the line on top in black, and your prediction as one red cross at distance 350. The line should run through the middle of the dots, and the cross should sit on it. Remember the difference: plt.scatter draws one dot per row and joins nothing; plt.plot joins its points in order into a line. Every value of line_speed lies on the same straight line, so the order of the rows does not matter.

Two errors to expect: Expected a 2-dimensional container means the distance needs its second pair of brackets; doesn't define __round__ means the slope needs its [0].

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: model, slope, intercept, line_speed and speed_350.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 6¶
docs.text:
How well does the line fit the supernovae?

Why: a line can be the best one and still be the wrong shape for its data. Two things tell you: a picture, the residual plot, the residuals drawn against distance; and one number, R².

R² compares your line with the simplest line there is, a flat one at the average speed, which ignores distance altogether:

$$R^2 = 1 - \left(\frac{\text{RMSE of the fitted line}}{\text{RMSE of the flat line}}\right)^2$$

It is 1 when every point sits on the line, and near 0 when the line does no better than the average. The flat line is the yardstick; it has no R² of its own here.

  1. residuals: the real speed minus line_speed, one for each supernova.
  2. The figure: the residuals against distance, as dots, with a horizontal line at zero to measure from. plt.axhline(0) draws one.
  3. line_rmse: the RMSE of the fitted line, as in section 2.
  4. flat_rmse: the RMSE of a flat line at the average speed: the residuals of that line are each speed minus the average speed.
  5. r_squared: by the equation, from the two RMSEs. The last line asks scikit-learn for the same number with model.score(x, y), which takes the same two things the fit was given.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: residuals, line_rmse, flat_rmse and r_squared.

docs.title: 4. How old does that make the universe?¶
docs.text:
This section uses slope from Your turn 5; run that cell again if you restarted.

A friend arrives at your door and says: "I drove 120 km at 60 km/h." You know when your friend left: 120 divided by 60, two hours ago. Time is distance divided by speed. The same works for a galaxy. If it has always moved at the speed it has today, the time since it was right here is

$$t = \frac{d}{v}$$

Hubble's law says $v = H_0 d$. Put that in, and the distance cancels:

$$t = \frac{d}{H_0 \, d} = \frac{1}{H_0}$$

The same time for every galaxy, near or far: they all set out together. So one over the slope is an age for the universe.

docs.title: ✏️ Your turn 7¶
docs.text:
Write the conversion once, as a function, and use it on both lines.

Why: you now have two lines, and the homework brings more. A function does the three steps in one call, for any slope.

  1. age_of_universe(hubble_constant): it takes a Hubble constant in km/s per Mpc and returns one over it, in billions of years. Its body is the three steps of the cell above, with hubble_constant in place of slope, and it ends with return, as your functions in the functions week did. The two constants are written again inside the function, so that it needs nothing from outside.
  2. age: call the function on your slope, the free line's.
  3. origin_model and H0_origin: fit the line through the origin, with fit_intercept=False as section 3 showed, and read its slope.
  4. age_origin: call the function on H0_origin.

Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: age_of_universe, age, origin_model, H0_origin and age_origin.

docs.title: The question, answered¶
docs.text: About 14 billion years. One over the slope of the best straight line through thirty-six supernovae gives 13.84 billion years when the line starts at zero, as Hubble's law says it must. The published age, from a model of the whole expansion, is 13.8 billion years. The close agreement is partly luck: 1/H₀ is a time of the right size, not the exact age, because the expansion has not been steady. The free line gave 14.48, and the Planck value of H₀ gives 14.51.

docs.title: The science¶
docs.text:
How old is the universe? A slope can be an age: the slope of speed against distance is how fast the universe expands, and one over it is a time. The best straight line has the smallest total of squared residuals. The physical model can also fix a point on it: Hubble's law has no intercept, so the line is fitted through the origin. Before trusting a line, draw it on its data and look at what it misses: R² is one number, and the residual plot shows whether there is a pattern.

  • Residual. A residual is the real value minus the line's value.
  • Linear regression. Draw the best straight line. Best means the smallest root mean squared error: the line that misses its points least.
  • Fit through the origin. When the physical model fixes a point on the line, the fit keeps it.

docs.text:

import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# house style, set once, so every plot cell below holds only what matters
plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110,
                     "axes.grid": True, "grid.alpha": 0.3, "axes.axisbelow": True})

CACHE = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AI4EPS/EPS88_PyEarth/main/data"

def load():

Why it rises. Burning coal, oil and gas, and clearing forests, release CO2. About half of what people emit stays in the air (48 percent over 2014–2023, by the Global Carbon Budget 2024); the oceans and the land take up the rest. Carbon is always moving between the air, plants, soils and the ocean; burning fossil fuels adds a flow that had no return path on human time scales.

The carbon cycle: where carbon is stored (black numbers, billions of tonnes) and how fast it moves (arrows, billions of tonnes a year). The numbers are from the 1990s; today the air holds more, and fossil fuels add more each year. The shape of the cycle is what matters here. Diagram: NASA Earth Observatory, redrawn by Kevin Saff and FischX (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons.

How unusual is today's level? Bubbles of old air trapped in the Antarctic ice sheet record CO2 long before anyone measured it. Through the ice ages of the last 800,000 years it swung from below 200 ppm in the coldest times to about 300 in the warmest, and it did not go above 300 until the industrial age:

CO2 over the last 800,000 years from ice cores, with the last thousand years enlarged; the steep black end is the age of measurements like Mauna Loa's. Figure: Femke Nijsse (CC BY-SA 3.0), via Wikimedia Commons.

Each year CO2 climbs to a high in May and falls to a low in September or October, and each high sits above the last. The yearly fall comes from plants. Most of the world's land that has a winter is in the northern half of the planet: forests and grasslands that green up together in spring and summer, taking CO2 out of the air, and lose their leaves together in autumn and winter, when decay gives it back. Mauna Loa, at 19.5° N, breathes with the north.

So a curve that follows this record needs two things: a rise that gets steeper, and a ripple that repeats every twelve months. The next section builds one piece at a time, and asks how to tell whether each piece helps.

Three sets, as for an exam. Think of studying:

  • the homework problems are what you learn from;
  • a practice exam tells you whether your way of studying works, and you may change your way of studying after seeing it;
  • the final exam is taken once, at the end. If you took it again and again, changing your answers each time, it would stop measuring what you know.

A model gets the same three sets of data, here three spans of years:

  • training months, 1958–2000: each curve learns from these;
  • validation months, 2001–2010: years held back to choose between models. Once they have chosen, they are no longer a fair test.
  • test months, 2011 onward: years nobody looks at until the end, checked once, on the model already chosen.

Why years in order, and not a random third of the months? Because a forecast is about the future. Months picked at random would sit between training months, where any smooth curve does well, and the test would say nothing about years to come. That would be leakage: any route by which information about the data you are scoring on reaches the model before you score it.

A new column lets a line-fitting method draw a curve. In the age-of-the-universe homework you gave the fit a second column, the distance squared. The fit finds one number for each column it is given, so with decades and decades squared it fits

The squared term is small near 1958 and grows fast later, which is exactly the shape of a rise that gets steeper. Nothing else changes: the same fit, the same masks, the same RMSE.

A wave repeats every twelve months, and two columns can draw one. Turn each month into an angle around a circle, one full turn a year: $\text{angle} = 2\pi \times (\text{month} - 0.5) / 12$. (A full turn is $2\pi$; the $-0.5$ puts each month at its middle.) The sine of that angle rises and falls once a year, and so does the cosine, a quarter of a year later. Drawn over twelve months:

The sine is highest in March and April and lowest in September and October; the cosine is highest in December and January and lowest in June and July. Give the fit both, and it chooses how much of each, which lets the mixed wave peak in any month and be any size. Each is a seasonal column: a column that rises and falls once a year, so the fitted curve can rise and fall with the seasons. The curve is now

$$\text{CO2} = a \times \text{decades} + c \times \text{decades}^2 + s \times \sin(\text{angle}) + k \times \cos(\text{angle}) + b$$

More columns always fit the training months better. They do not always fit new months better. The squared curve with seasons misses the validation decade by only 0.77 ppm. Why stop there? A cubed column, or a fourth power, would bend the curve more freely and fit 1958–2000 even more closely. The risk has a name, overfitting: a curve that memorises the data you gave it fails on the data you did not. The highest power in a curve is its degree: the degree of a polynomial is how many bends it is allowed: degree 1 is a straight line, degree 2 bends once.

The way to find out is to try each degree and score it on the validation months. The figure that shows the answer is a validation curve: plot the miss on the training years and on the held-back years against how flexible the curve is; the flexibility worth choosing is where the held-back miss is lowest.

The two lines tell different stories. On the training months every extra power helps, or at least does no harm: 1.92, 0.97, 0.82 and 0.82 ppm. On the validation months the squared curve wins clearly, 0.77 ppm, and the cubed and fourth-power curves are four to six times worse (4.51 and 3.31). The extra powers let the curve follow small bends in the 1958–2000 record, which buys almost nothing there (from 0.97 to 0.82 ppm), and then carry those bends forward into years where they do not belong: in the figure, the cubed and fourth-power curves fall below the data after 2001. That is overfitting, seen in the data rather than described.

The two ways to fail have names. Too simple and you miss the pattern; too flexible and you memorise the noise. The line is too simple: it misses the bend everywhere (bias). The cubed and fourth-power curves are too flexible: what they learn depends on the accidents of the years they were given (variance). The squared curve sits between them.

Think. If you had chosen by the training RMSE alone, which curve would you have picked?

docs.title: When will CO2 pass 450 ppm?¶
docs.text:
EPS 88 · PyEarth. Open your own copy on DataHub: click here.

Every month since March 1958, an observatory high on Mauna Loa, a volcano in Hawaii, has measured how much carbon dioxide (CO2) is in the air. It is the longest record of its kind, and its yearly average has gone up every single year. It now stands near 430 parts per million. When will it pass 450?

To answer, you need a curve that follows the record, and a fair way to tell a curve that has learned the pattern from one that has only memorised the past. Today you fit four curves, choose between them on years they never saw, test the winner once on the most recent years, and read its forecast. Then you see how much that forecast depends on the choice. At home you repeat the method at two more stations, one in the Arctic and one at the South Pole.

Every place you write something opens with a pencil icon and the words Your turn, and is followed by a cell that already has the shape of the answer written in, with ... wherever your code goes. Replace every ..., run every cell so your answers and figures are saved in the file, then download this notebook itself — the .ipynb file — and upload it to Gradescope. Not a PDF: the marking reads your notebook, and a PDF cannot be read. In JupyterLab: File ▸ Download, or right-click the file in the left-hand panel and choose Download.

Two habits from the first minute. A cell runs when you press Shift+Enter, and the notebook remembers everything it has already run — so when something breaks and you cannot see why, Kernel → Restart Kernel and Run All Cells throws the memory away and rebuilds it from the top. That is never the wrong thing to do.

docs.title: What you'll be able to do¶
docs.text:
The science. Describe the two patterns in the CO2 record, the long rise and the yearly breath; say when the yearly average reaches 450 ppm by the curve the data choose; and explain why that date is less certain than the fit makes it look.

The code. A new column made from an old one (a square, a sine, a cosine) · fitting on training months, choosing on validation months, testing once · a loop that compares four models · np.sin, np.cos and np.pi.

Thirteen places where you write something: nine in class, four at home. Each is headed Your turn, and the cell under it has the shape of the answer written in, with ... wherever your code goes and a comment beside each one saying what goes there.

The four questions of the class:

  1. What does the CO2 record show?
  2. How do we choose a curve we can trust on years it has not seen?
  3. When will CO2 pass 450 ppm?
  4. How far can we trust that answer?

docs.title: Setup¶
docs.text:
Run the next cell once. It reads NOAA's Mauna Loa file (live if the network is up, the copy stored with the course if not) and the two stations for the homework, which are stored with the course. Then it adds two columns to each table:

  • time: the middle of each month, written as a year with decimals (March 1958 is 1958.21);
  • decades: the time since 1958, counted in decades (2026 is 6.8 decades).

Counting in decades keeps the numbers small. Later you will square this column and take higher powers of it; counted in years, the fourth power of 2026's value would be about 20 million, far too large for the fit to handle well.

(The numbers quoted in this notebook come from the stored copy; if your notebook read NOAA's live file, a few may differ in their last digit.)

docs.title: 1. What does the CO2 record show?¶
docs.text:
CO2 is counted in parts per million. A reading of 430 ppm means that in every million molecules of air, 430 are carbon dioxide. That is a small share, but CO2 lets sunlight in and holds back some of the heat the ground gives off. It is one of the gases behind the greenhouse effect from the liquid-water week: the difference between the temperature a world would have with no air and the temperature it actually has.

Where the numbers come from. Charles David Keeling began measuring CO2 on Mauna Loa in March 1958. The observatory sits 3,397 m up the volcano's side, far from cities and forests, so the air it samples has mixed over a wide area; one station there tells you about much of the planet.

The Mauna Loa Observatory on the volcano's bare lava slope. Photo: Brian Vasel, NOAA (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons.
